questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design runtime-extensible routing logic for streaming with low-latency and backpressure concerns. Requires a registry for pluggable policies, a clean, minimal interface, and non-blocking paths to sinks. Examines tradeoffs between hot vs cold storage and observability.

## Key Concepts

- Strategy pattern
- Registry and runtime extensibility
- Backpressure and non-blocking IO
- Hot-swapping configuration

## Code Example

```ts
interface Message { source: string; schema: string; ttl: number }
interface Sink { enqueue(msg: Message): Promise<void> }
interface RoutingPolicy { selectSink(msg: Message): Sink }
class PolicyRegistry { register(name: string, policy: RoutingPolicy): void; get(name: string): RoutingPolicy | undefined }
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test hot-swapped policies without risking data loss?
- How do you ensure observability across multiple sinks when routing fails?

## Why This Is Asked
This question probes real-world extensibility: adding rules without redeploying, and per-message routing based on metadata.

## Key Concepts
- Runtime plugin architecture with a Registry
- Minimal Rule interface: apply(Message) -> Result
- Per-message pipeline construction from metadata
- Safe dynamic loading and testing

```javascript
interface Message { region:string; product:string; tier:string; payload:any }
interface Result { ok:boolean; errors?:string[] }
interface Rule { apply(msg:Message):Result }
class Registry { register(name:string, r:Rule):void; get(name:string):Rule | undefined }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle rule versioning and rollback?
- What are the trade-offs of eager vs lazy loading of rules?

## Why This Is Asked
Shows how to design pluggable, runtime-extendable policy logic for high-stakes API gateways while avoiding restarts. Tests hot-swap safety and ordering guarantees.


## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle rule dependencies and initialization order?
- How would you test hot-reload without affecting live traffic?

- Strategy, Registry, Atomic swap, Per-tenant policy
- Thread-safety, hot-swapping, migration
- Trade-offs: memory vs flexibility

```javascript
// pseudo
interface RateLimitStrategy { allow(req): boolean }
class TokenBucket implements RateLimitStrategy {...}
class RateLimiter { Map tenants->RateLimitStrategy; Registry<String,Supplier<RateLimitStrategy>> registry }
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How to persist tenant policies across restarts?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates the ability to design for runtime extensibility and reliability in a pluggable notification system.

## Key Concepts

- **Registry-driven plugins**: Channels are registered at runtime via a central registry, enabling new channel types without recompiling the core dispatcher.
- **Channel interface and factories**: A standardized contract ensures all notification channels implement common behavior while factories handle instantiation.
- **Per-user preferences**: Respect individual user settings for preferred notification channels and delivery priority.
- **Fallback strategy**: A reliable rollback mechanism ensures notifications are delivered even when primary channels fail.
